 AI may be coming for the org chart. Airbnb CEO Brian Chesky says employees who resist change or only manage people could struggle to keep up.
 Nucleus_AI 4194 Stories Monday October 26, 2026 , 3 min Read 
 AI may not take your job. But refusing to change how you work could put you at risk.
 As artificial intelligence reshapes workplaces, Airbnb CEO Brian Chesky believes the biggest risk may not come down to which industry someone works in, but how willing they are to adapt.
 Speaking on the Invest Like The Best podcast, Brian Chesky identified two groups that could struggle as companies change: managers who only manage people, and employees who resist new ways of working.
 His statements centre on a workplace where AI can take on more routine tasks, leaving employees and managers to contribute through stronger judgement, practical skills and the ability to improve how work gets done.
 Why ‘pure people managers’ could be at risk
 Brian Chesky’s first concern is what he calls “pure people managers”. These are managers whose responsibilities largely revolve around supervising teams, conducting meetings and holding one-on-one conversations, without directly contributing to the work.
 He argued that this kind of management role could become less valuable if leaders do little beyond coordinating people and processes.
 Instead, Chesky sees managers taking on a more hands-on role. He described the future manager as a “hybrid people manager” or a “manager IC”, combining team leadership with the responsibilities of an individual contributor.
 That means managers would still need to support employees and build strong working relationships, but they would also be expected to understand the work itself and help teams improve its quality.
 The second risk: Refusing to adapt
 The other group Chesky highlighted comprises people who are rigid and unwilling to change. As AI tools become part of everyday workflows, employees who resist learning new systems or experimenting with different approaches may struggle to keep up. 
 By contrast, those willing to learn may be better placed to adapt as job requirements evolve. The distinction is not necessarily between people who understand AI and those who do not. It is between those who remain open to learning and those who assume their existing skills and methods will always be enough.
 Across industries, AI is increasingly being used for tasks such as writing, coding, research, analysis and customer support. As these capabilities expand, employees may need to focus more on judgement, creativity and applying their expertise effectively.
 What Jony Ive has to do with it
 During the discussion, Brian pointed to former Apple chief design officer Jony Ive as an example of someone who combines deep craft with leadership. 
 The reference reinforces Chesky’s opinion that effective managers should understand the work their teams produce, rather than limiting themselves to meetings, calendars and workplace morale.
 People management remains important, but he argues that leaders should also help employees solve problems and raise the standard of their output.

 Adaptability could become a career advantage
 Brian Chesky’s view is not that everyone needs to become an AI expert overnight. Rather, employees need to remain willing to learn and explore how new tools can improve their work.
 For businesses, this could mean rethinking management roles and investing in continuous learning. For employees, it means treating existing expertise as a foundation to build on, rather than a reason to resist change.
 AI may automate some tasks and reshape others. But as Chesky’s comments suggest, the ability to adapt could matter just as much as the technology itself.
